Items.Authors: Aman Chandra, Hina Suzuki, Heejoo Choi, Adrien Bouskela, Walter Rahmer, Daewook Kim, Christopher Walker
Items.Title: A scalable rigidized inflatable reflector system for next-generation far-infrared space telescopes
Items.Abstract: Inflatable membrane reflectors offer a compelling pathway to realizing large-aperture optical systems for far-infrared and millimeter-wave astronomy. Compared with mechanically deployed reflectors, membrane-based systems provide exceptional advantages in mass efficiency, stowage volume, scalability, and structural simplicity. Our work introduces a novel, instrumentation-driven approach that directly addresses these historical limitations. Central to this approach is an optical architecture that pairs an inflatable primary membrane mirror with precision-machined corrective surfaces, enabling compensation for low-order membrane aberrations and improved far-IR wavefront quality. These innovations are being implemented and validated on a 3-meter prototype reflector, which serves as a critical testbed for understanding inflation behavior, tension-load paths, rigidization performance, and metrology-informed surface correction strategies.

Items.Authors: Nuwanthika Fernando, Brent Miszalski, Nuria Lorente, Anthony Horton
Items.Title: MAVIS- Final design of the data reduction pipeline
Items.Abstract: MAVIS is the MCAO Assisted Visible Imager and Spectrograph, the first MCAO-facility instrument planned for the VLT which will provide a near diffraction-limited view of the visible wavelength. We present the final design for the Data Reduction Pipeline of the instrument, and describe the prototyping for the design of calibration methods and dataflows. For the spectrograph calibrations, the geometry of the slices is determined using a series of moving pinhole mask exposures. Prototyping the geometry recipe resulted in the change to the pinhole mask design. This also confirmed the need for etalons for the wavelength calibration, to achieve required accuracies in the low resolution blue mode. Early prototyping of the DRS has been beneficial to the design of the entire instrument. The critical algorithms used ESO’s PyCPL libraries, the GNU Scientific Library, and data workflows at each stage were drafted using the new EDPS (ESO Data Processing System) libraries.

Items.Authors: André J. van Es, Mark Waterson, Robert Haigh, Ivan Lloro, Randall Wayth, Lucio Tirone, Luca Stringhetti, Robert Laing, Alan Davis, Raunaq Bhushan, Pieter Benthem, Marco Caiazzo, Giulia Macario, Shinichiro Asayama, Jess Broderick, Maria Grazia Labate, Danny Price, Maciej Serylak, Riley Keel, Charlotte Sobey, Jimi Green, Ravi Subrahmanyan, Bartosz Idzkowski, Jader Monari, Gianni Bernardi, Pietro Bolli, Carolina Belli, Letizia Caito, Simone Chiarucci, Giovanni Comoretto, Paola Di Ninni, Andrea Mattana, Federico Perini, Giuseppe Pupillo, Marco Schiaffino, Monica Alderighi, Carlo Baffa, Sergio D'Angelo, Davide Fierro, Elisabeth Giani, Giovanni Naldi, Marco Poloni, Simone Rusticelli, Francesco Schiliro, Federica Caputo, Tom Booler, David Davidson, Dave Minchin, Andy McPhail, Maria Kovaleva, Marcin Sokolowski, Jishnu N. Thekkeppattu, Steven Tingay, Daniel Ung, Angela Teale, Kris Zarb Adami, Raphael Thenevin, Aniket Hendre, Jan Geralt Bij de Vaate
Items.Title: The road to SKA-Low from a station prototype to a system prototype, covering the journey from AAVS1 until SKA-Low AA0.5
Items.Abstract: This presentation shows a comprehensive overview of the prototyping and verification activities that laid the foundation for the construction of the SKA-Low telescope. It traces the evolution from early experimental platforms (AAVS1-3) culminating in the deployment of the first four fully integrated SKA-Low stations (AA0.5). These stations, delivered as part of the AA0.5 milestone, bring together all essential subsystems of the telescope—from antennas and digitisation to signal processing and control—demonstrating end-to-end functionality at scale. The paper highlights key technical achievements, lessons learned, and the critical role of prototyping in de-risking design decisions ahead of full array construction.

Items.Authors: Zi-hang Zhu, Ze-yu Zhu, Zhi-hao Cao, Feng Li, Bao-long Chen, Jian Wang
Items.Title: WFST-ChatOps: A Domain-Adapted QA Chatbot for the Wide Field Survey Telescope
Items.Abstract: Artificial intelligence and large language models are reshaping how humans access knowledge, collaborate on complex projects, and support critical operations. For large scientific facilities, AI assistants can help operators understand system design and obtain guidance during routine procedures and incidents.The Mozi Wide Field Survey Telescope (WFST) is a wide-field time-domain survey facility with a sophisticated hardware–software stack, creating a strong need for tools that support observation operations with reliable domain knowledge. In this work we construct a specialized question–answer dataset covering scenario-based queries on project explanations and day-to-day operations, and we use DeepSeek-R1-32B model via parameter-efficient fine-tuning to obtain WFST-ChatOps（Chat-Operations）, a domain-oriented QA chatbot that provides natural-language access to WFST project information, design reports, and operation manuals.

Items.Authors: David Murphy
Items.Title: COMCUBE-S: a CubeSat swarm for GRB polarimetry and localisation
Items.Abstract: COMCUBE-S is a proposed CubeSat swarm mission designed to provide polarisation measurements of Gamma-Ray Burst prompt emission as well as all-sky monitoring for high-energy time domain astronomy, with rapid alert notifications in response to high energy transients.    The mission consists of 28 16U CubeSats. Each satellite carries an advanced miniaturised Compton telescope allowing COMCUBE-S to make temporal, spectral, and polarimetric measurements of gamma-rays in the tens of keV to a few MeV range    The swarm satellites will be equally distributed along an equatorial orbit, forming a closed ring of intersatellite links. Satellites in the swarm are able to identify high-energy transients, relay data to the ground and distribute source locations to observatories worldwide for follow-up. COMCUBE-S will localise 160 GRBs per year with positions distributed within 120 s.    The project has completed a Phase A study with ESA and aims to launch a two-satellite in-orbit demonstarion by 2030.

Items.Authors: Kenichi Karatsu, Shahab Dabironezare, Louis Marting, Leon Olde Scholtenhuis, Daniela Perez Capelo, David Thoen, Alejandro Pascual Laguna, Sten Vollebregt, Akira Endo, Jochem Baselmans
Items.Title: Development of broadband spectro-polarimetric arrays for next-generation CMB observations
Items.Abstract: A new spectro-polarimeter array has been developed for next-generation Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) instruments. The design features 14 spatial pixels, each consisting of a polarization-separating broadband leaky-wave lens-antenna, with each single-polarization output connected to a high-sensitivity, low-resolution 22-channel mm/sub-mm on-chip filterbank operating in a frequency range from 135–270 GHz. The device uses kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs) to detect the power in each spectral band. The array with ~600 KIDs was fabricated and measured, demonstrating a cross-polarization level lower than –15 dB and an averaged filter peak efficiency of 67%. The design is compact and scalable towards larger arrays. The results show promise for achieving a large-format spectro-polarimetric focal plane array for future CMB instruments.

Items.Authors: Ronald Holzlöhner, Michael Esselborn, Xavier Ariño, Henri Bonnet, Martin Brinkmann, Juan-Carlos González-Herrera, Michael Müller, Christophe Vérinaud
Items.Title: Impact of dome seeing in ESO’s ELT on wide-field wavefront correction
Items.Abstract: We are running end-to-end simulations based on transient aerothermal computational fluid dynamics (CFD) of the entire ESO’s ELT telescope, dome and surrounding air volume.    Dome seeing is challenging to AO: spider seeing can drive pupil fragmentation, also known as the petaling effect. Secondly, most of the dome turbulence is optically conjugated to heights between zero and −300 m. Since M4, the telescope deformable mirror (DM), is conjugated to +620 m and secondary DMs are conjugated to even higher altitudes, the WF delivered by the telescope suffers from increasing uncorrectable errors vs. field angle.    The present work refines our previous CFD simulation as follows: We include a) additional open louvers in the dome, b) free convection by adding a buoyancy term to the equations, c) simplified mountain orography model and non-uniform temperature at the dome inlet, d) holes in M1 due to missing segments. We are investigating the WFE at field angles 0–4 arcmin off axis from LGS and NGS.

Items.Authors: Locke D. Spencer, Christopher Benson, Thomas Essenger-Hileman, William Grainger, David Leisawitz, Lee Mundy, Ettore Pedretti, Berke V. Ricketti, Giorgio Savini, Jeremy P. Scott, Gerard van Belle, David Wilner
Items.Title: Technology development for space-based far-infrared double Fourier interferometry
Items.Abstract: Many fundamental questions leading astrophysics research require observations with high resolution spectroscopy and imaging at high spatial resolution, i.e., hyper-spectral imaging, in the Far-Infrared (Far-IR). Topics include: the origin of the universe, conditions for star and planet formation, and, ultimately, the conditions for the emergence of life. Over half of the energy emitted by the Universe appears in the relatively unexplored Far-IR spectral region, most of which is opaque from ground-based sites necessitating space-borne instrumentation.   We discuss the motivating science and technology development supporting Far-IR Double Fourier Interferometry instrumentation, requisite components, and associated technology requisite for the advancement of a Far-IR Double Fourier Interferometry space mission. This includes development of digital simulation tools, laboratory instrumentation development and demonstration, and exploration of the science potential of such a facility.

Items.Authors: James P. Gill-Fleming, Meryem K. Dağ, Kieran S. O'Brien
Items.Title: qCMOS Single photon counting spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: Modern quantitative CMOS (qCMOS) detectors now achieve sub-electron readout noise, enabling photon-number-resolving performance in compact, room-temperature system without the complexity associated with superconducting or avalanche-photodiode detectors. We demonstrate single-photon counting spectroscopy using the Hamamatsu ORCA-Quest 2, a 4k qCMOS camera (~0.27 e⁻ RMS) integrated with a modest imaging spectrograph (380–750 nm, R≈2300). Per-pixel readout-noise maps and dark-current analysis define the operational limits of large-format qCMOS in the photon-counting regime. Low-flux tests show clear photon-number peak separation and linear spectral response at the single-photon level. These results establish qCMOS as a practical, accessible detector technology for next-generation photon-limited astronomical instruments.

Items.Authors: Guido Cupani
Items.Title: Astrocook v2: LLM-Ready Foundation for Autonomous Analysis of Quasar Spectra
Items.Abstract: Astrocook v2 represents a major architectural redesign of the well-known quasar analysis tool. It is built on an immutable data core, a decoupled API, and a new PySide6 GUI. This system guarantees stability, high performance, and readiness for external integration.    We highlight the successful implementation of a robust SciPy-based Voigt Fitter and a powerful Parameter Constraints workflow. This system enables full parameter linking (Value/Thermal modes) and dynamic evaluation. The core strength is reproducible, controlled analysis, supported by the SystemListV2 as the Single Source of Truth for component grouping and the interactive System Inspector for efficient component manipulation.    This stable foundation, with its immutable API and fully constrained physical model, is engineered for integration with Large Language Models (LLMs). Astrocook will leverage AI reasoning for guiding complex analysis sequences, advancing toward autonomous pipelines for future spectroscopic surveys.

Items.Authors: Sayuf Shaik, Kathiravan C., Ramesh R., Gireesh G.V.S., Indrajit Barve, Rajesh M.
Items.Title: Augmentation of Gauribidanur Radioheliograph for simultaneous total intensity and circular polarisation imaging of solar corona at low radio frequencies
Items.Abstract: The coronal magnetic field is predominant in forming structures such as streamers, holes, etc., and in determining their spatio-temporal evolution. Its routine estimation will most likely provide clues/answers to several unsolved problems in solar physics. In this view, we started commissioning a dedicated radio facility to routinely measure B in the corona, particularly in the 1.2 - 2.0 solar radio heliocentric distance range. For that, the existing Gauribidanur RAdioheliograPH (GRAPH) of the Gauribidanur radio observatory is being augmented to image the circularly polarized radio emission, in addition to total intensity in the 30 - 130 MHz frequency range. The necessary analog and digital receivers, reconfiguration, data processing pipelines were built and characterized. The computer algorithms based on the ray-tracing technique are also being developed to reproduce the observed images and help in coronal magnetic field estimation.

Items.Authors: Leanne P. Guy, Connor Yablonski, Aaron Meisner, Guillem Megias Homar, Merlin Fisher-Levine, Christopher W. Stubbs
Items.Title: Development of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation Chatbot for Enhanced Information Discovery at Rubin Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s LSST will produce petabytes of data supported by a large, heterogeneous set of technical documents, operational guides, and scientific notes. Because this material is distributed across numerous platforms and formats, including internal systems, users and general-purpose language models often find it difficult to locate reliable Rubin-specific information. To address this, we developed a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) virtual assistant that provides context-aware, factual access to Rubin’s documentation ecosystem. The system aggregates content from multiple sources and performs semantic search through a conversational interface, using Weaviate for embeddings, LangChain for query orchestration, and an OpenAI GPT model as the LLM backend. Grounding responses in domain-specific knowledge reduces hallucinations, improves accuracy, and demonstrates the potential of RAG to streamline workflows and support effective use of LSST data products.

Items.Authors: Takumi Hagiwara, Subaru Shibai, Yutaro Enomoto, Kiwamu Izumi
Items.Title: Telescope of lossless intersatellite laser ranging for the SILVIA formation flying mission
Items.Abstract: This work proposes an optical telescope architecture for intersatellite laser interferometry missions SILVIA, where lossless intersatellite laser ranging is employed.    To simplify link acquisition and reduce reliance on satellite attitude control, we propose a non-cooperative laser link approach. However, this approach poses two major challenges: both retroreflection and mode matching must be simultaneously achieved, and sharing a single telescope for transmission and reception makes independent bidirectional alignment nontrivial.    To overcome these issues, we propose a new telescope design inspired by the cat’s-eye retroreflector and derive its parameters using ray-matrix analysis. Based on this design, we are currently developing an optical breadboard model (BBM). This talk presents the design concept and reports on the current BBM development status.

Items.Authors: Miska Le Louarn, Julio A. Castro-Almazán, Donaji Esparza-Arredondo, Maria Begoña García-Lorenzo, Johann Kolb, Angel C. Otarola, Jerome Paufique, Camila de Sa Freitas
Items.Title: Comparing turbulence outer scale measurements on-sky between LGS-WFS data and MUSE image-cubes at the VLT
Items.Abstract: The Outer scale of turbulence (L0) will play a significant role in the performance of Adaptive Optics (AO) instruments at the ELT, especially those based on laser guide stars (LGS), through the distribution of turbulent power in the low order modes. It is therefore important to understand this parameter.  In this talk, we will present results from a measurement campaign at the Very Large Telescope (VLT) at Paranal Observatory to measure simultaneously the outer scale through two independent methods. The first method is based on LGS wavefront sensor measurements, using the AO facility (AOF). The second method relies on the variation of image quality (IQ) with wavelength at the focal plane of the MUSE Integral Field Spectrograph (IFS) in its Wide Field Mode (MUSE-WFM).  We compare the L0 values obtained through the two methods, using different AO modes. With weak TT correction we find a very good correlation between the two methods, giving confidence in their accuracy.

Items.Authors: Emily M. Witt, Brian T. Fleming, Stephan McCandliss, Isu Ravi, Vida Saeedzadeh, Jason Tumlinson, Sarah Tuttle, Cassandra Lochhaas, Matilde Mingozzi, Briana Indahl, Manuel Quijada
Items.Title: The Juniper CubeSat: mission operations
Items.Abstract: The circumgalactic media (CGM) of galaxies play a key role in the baryon cycle of galactic feedback. Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the CGM in particular is crucial to understanding the flow of gas and metals into and out of galaxies. To characterize this process, the Juniper 16U CubeSat mission has been designed to conduct observations of the CGM of nearby galaxies in multiple far ultraviolet (FUV) bandpasses that include key metal lines such as O VI (103.5 nm), C II (133.5 nm), and C IV (154.9 nm). Juniper will observe the CGM of roughly ten galaxies and will conduct weekly calibration observations to characterize the performance of the new FUV technologies that enable Juniper's unprecedented spectral resolution. This proceedings will overview the current mission status and discuss the planned mission operations for Juniper.

Items.Authors: Samantha Walker, Austin Kaczmarek, Douglas Bennett, Darshan Patel, Jason Austermann, Shannon Duff, Johannes Hubmayr, Kelsey Morgan, Dan Schmidt, Daniel Swetz, Joel Ullom, Anna Vaskuri, Michael Vissers, Joel Weber, Jordan Wheeler, Michael Niemack, Katja Nowack
Items.Title: Visualizing the properties of astronomical superconducting detectors with scanning SQUID microscopy
Items.Abstract: Large arrays of superconducting detectors, such as transition-edge sensors (TESs) and kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs), are being used in an increasing number of experiments across the electromagnetic spectrum. However, there remain gaps in our understanding of detector physics. Using scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy (SSM), we directly visualize (sub)millimeter and X-ray TESs and KIDs with micrometer-scale spatial resolution at sub-Kelvin temperatures. For TESs, we image a direct superconducting proximity effect, where the TES acts as a weak link between superconducting leads, and an inverse proximity effect with normal metal structures. We visualize the current distribution in voltage-biased TESs. For KIDs, we directly image vortex configurations in different regions of the device. Our work has implications for understanding how design choices affect TES and KID operation and aims to lead to more optimal arrays for future observatories.

Items.Authors: Brenda Aurea Cervantes Vergara
Items.Title: Skipcam: a Skipper-CCD array for ultra-low-noise wide-field astronomy
Items.Abstract: Skipcam is a 5x4 array of blue-sensitive skipper-CCDs developed as a technology demonstrator for future large, ultra-low-noise astronomical focal planes. The 20-sensor raft matches the mechanical interface of the WIYN 3.5-m telescope, representing 1/16 of a full-scale focal plane and enabling a realistic path to survey-class instrumentation. Skipcam will operate on the 0.61-m aperture Curtis–Schmidt telescope at CTIO to validate mechanical integration, thermal performance, alignment, and multiplexed readout. Five MIDNA ASICs, providing dual-slope processing and multiplexing, and a compact backend read out the full array. Skipcam will enable applications such as microlensing surveys, DESI-2/Spec-S5 targeting, wide-field fast imaging, and multi-messenger astrophysics follow-up.

Items.Authors: Laurane Fréour, Anna Puglisi, Amelia Bayo, Fatemeh Zahra Majidi, Sabine Thater, Francesca Primas, Laurence Tresse, Umberto Rescigno, Daniela Iglesias Vallejo, Stephanie Escoffier, Maria Cristina Fortuna
Items.Title: Embedding Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion in the WST collaboration
Items.Abstract: Astronomy, and STEM disciplines more broadly, are characterized by the underrepresentation of marginalized groups, particularly in leadership positions. Integrating Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) principles is essential for any large-scale collaboration or project.  The proposed Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST) is a next-generation telescope facility with a 12-meter primary mirror that may be operational in the 2040s. The project gathers more than 1000 science community members, spanning multiple time zones and a broad range of scientific goals.  From the project's initial phases, the WST sought to embed DEI considerations, aiming to deliver groundbreaking scientific results while serving as a model for integrating diversity into decision-making and project development. Multiple strategies are being implemented to advance DEI and cultivate a sustainable work environment, such as inclusive leadership training and DEI seminars.

Items.Authors: Ruslan Belikov, Dan Sirbu, Eduardo Bendek, David Marx, Camilo Mejia Prada, Hanying Zhou, Byong-Joon Seo, Jonathan W. Lin, Kevin F. Sims
Items.Title: Multi-star wavefront control: updates on science opportunities for Roman CGI and HWO, and latest progress in technology development
Items.Abstract: This work presents the latest technology development and science opportunities for Multi-Star Wavefront Control (MSWC), a method to enable high-contrast imaging of multi-star systems with the Roman Space Telescope and Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). MSWC enhances the exoplanet yield and enables new science specific to planets around multi-star systems. In addition, it enables a follow up of the aCenA planet candidate recently reported by JWST. Our laboratory tests are continuing at JPL’s High Contrast Imaging Testbed (HCIT), and at time of this writing, include a demonstration of 9.4e-8 in full MSWC mode for an equivalent aCenAB separation. Scaled to the binary’s actual flux ratio, these performance levels yield equivalent contrasts of 3.7e-8 (aCenA) and 1.8e-7 (aCenB). These results suggest that current performance may already be sufficient to detect planets around aCenA in reflected light, if it can be replicated on sky.

Items.Authors: Parker T. Johnson, Jared R. Males, Laird M. Close, Olivier Guyon, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Joseph D. Long, Jay K. Kueny, Maggie Y. Kautz, Jialin Li, Joshua I. Liberman, Miles D. Lucas, Matthijs Mars, Eden A. McEwen, Tiffany Nguyen, Elena Tonucci, Katie Twitchell
Items.Title: Sensor fusion on MagAO-X: real time vibration control using accelerometers
Items.Abstract: Mechanical vibrations significantly impact wavefront error (WFE) in ground-based adaptive optics (AO) systems, requiring stellar photons for correction. This reduces bandwidth available for correcting atmospheric turbulence and makes corrections dependent on guide star brightness. To address this, we implemented a low-cost solution to mitigate vibrations for current and future ground-based AO systems, including the GMT. We mounted on the secondary mirror of the 6.5m Clay Magellan telescope and the MagAO-X optical table to directly measure vibrations. These accelerometers feed real-time data to the MagAO-X system, enabling vibration control independent of guide star brightness. Our system processes signals through a low-latency pipeline and improves WFE correction for tip, tilt, and focus. We show vibrations account for roughly 35% of the power in both tip and tilt in closed loop WFS measurements. This will result in a more stable optical system allowing us to detect fainter companions.

Items.Authors: Angelique Barbier, Wilhem Roux, Paolo Tanga
Items.Title: The CNES at the service of Solar System modelling by Gaia data
Items.Abstract: ESA's Gaia mission, launched in 2013, aims to create the most accurate 3D map of the Milky Way by observing 1.8 billion celestial objects. Although not optimized for solar system object (SSO) detection, Gaia has provided position measurements 100 times more precise than previous decades. Data processing is handled by the European DPAC consortium and SSO processing is done in Toulouse, at CNES.    Gaia contributes to SSO science in two ways: daily and cyclic processing. Daily processing detects relative movements against stars, calculates orbital solutions for unidentified objects, and sends alerts to observatories for new observations, enabling discoveries. Cyclic processing, ongoing, compares calculated SSO positions with Gaia-observed sources.     The paper will revisit the identification of scientific challenges, processing design, and the human organization implemented for SSOs processing

Items.Authors: Boudewijn Hut, Carla J. Baldovin Saveedra, Cees Bassa, Ilse van Bemmel, André Gunst, Tom Kamphuis, Ronald Roelfsema, John Swinbank, Sander ter Veen
Items.Title: Towards the LOFAR2.0 Observatory: our engineering journey
Items.Abstract: The world's largest low-frequency (10-250MHz) radio telescope is undergoing a major upgrade of its hardware, firmware and software to improve its unique observing capabilities. A variety of scientific use cases, ranging from galaxy evolution, transients and cosmic rays to space weather and lightning research is targeted. This pan-European Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR) is continuously improved by ASTRON and its partners to keep it a world class telescope.     Given the science goals of the LOFAR2.0 upgrade, we present an overview of the main design challenges and key solutions by our multi-disciplinary team: from antenna, mechanical, network and software to systems engineering and high-performance computing. We also present our approach to integrate the solutions into the new LOFAR2.0 Observatory.

Items.Authors: Zhenyuan Sun, Stafford Withington, Songyuan Zhao, Wei Chen
Items.Title: Analysis of resonance circular distortions in superconducting resonators against two dissipative nonlinear models at low and high readout power regimes
Items.Abstract: Experimental measurements of superconducting microwave resonators reveal distinct distortions of the resonance circle in the complex plane: a ‘teardrop’ shape at low readout power and a ‘squashed’ shape at high power. We compare these observations with two representative dissipative models—the two-level system (TLS) model at low power and quasiparticle heating (QPH) at high power. Both models show reasonable agreement with the measured distortions: TLS accurately reproduces the low-power teardrop, while QPH closely matches the high-power squashed morphology. Although other mechanisms may contribute in general at high power ranges, they are not necessary to explain the data presented here. These results demonstrate that resonance-circle morphology, when combined with dissipative models, serves as a practical diagnostic tool for identifying dominant loss behaviour in superconducting resonators for cryogenic detector and readout applications.

Items.Authors: Yuri Evangelista, Francesco Ceraudo, Giovanni Della Casa, Ettore Del Monte, Giuseppe Dilillo, Marco Feroci, Edoardo Giancarli, Alessio Nuti, Riccardo Campana, Mauro Fiorini, Giovanni Lombardi, Massimo Rapisarda, Ajay Sharma, Giuseppe Bertuccio, Filippo Mele, Yinhe Zhu, Marco Grassi, Piero Malcovati, Jacopo Giani, Marco Tambussi, Matias Antonelli, Alexandre Rachevski, Irina Rashevskaya, Gianluigi Zampa, Nicola Zampa, Evgeny Demenev, Giancarlo Pepponi, Francesco Ficorella, Nicola Zorzi, Francesca Esposito, Immacolata Donnarumma, Alessandro Turchi, Ugo Cortesi, Fabio D'Amico, Marco Gai, Andrea Argan
Items.Title: LEM-X: an all sky monitor for the Moon's surface
Items.Abstract: LEM-X is an all-sky X-ray observatory proposed for the surface of the Moon. Its primary scientific goal is to enhance multi-messenger astrophysics by detecting and monitoring high-energy transient phenomena and variable X-ray sources across the sky.  The building block of LEM-X is a pair of coded aperture cameras, able to image the sky in a field of view of 2sr (FWZR) with a source location accuracy of 1 arcmin. The LEM-X instrument envisages multiple camera pairs in a dome-shaped structure, with each camera designed to achieve a sensitivity better than 5 mCrab in 50ks and 1 Crab in 1s in a wide energy band (2-50 keV).  The sensitive elements of LEM-X are large area linear Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs) read-out by custom low-noise ASICs, which provide excellent spectral-timing performance. The energy resolution at room temperature is better than 350 eV FWHM at 6 keV, with 10 us time resolution.  In this contribution we describe the LEM-X design and report about its development status.

Items.Authors: Giuseppe Sottile, Pierluca Sangiorgi, Fabio Lo Gerfo, Carmelo Gargano, Mattia Corpora, Davide Mollica, Giovanni Contino, Teresa Mineo, Giovanni Pareschi, Michele Buzzi, Salvatore Scuderi, Antonio Miccichè, Giuseppe Leto, Gaetano Nicotra, Eugenio Martinetti, Giancarlo Bellassai, Michele Bellassai, Carmelo Lauretta, Salvatore Garozzo, Davide Marano, Andrea Abba, Francesco Caponio, Alberto Cusimano, Julien Fleury, Florent Perez, Salleh Ahmad, Jean Baptiste Cizel, Gino Tosti
Items.Title: First results from the ASTRI Mini-Array air-Cherenkov cameras
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array, led by INAF, will deploy nine dual-mirror air-Cherenkov telescopes at the Teide Observatory (Tenerife), using the Schwarzschild–Couder configuration. Seven telescopes are installed, with two already acquiring Cherenkov data during commissioning and science verification. The ASTRI camera features a 10.5° Field of View and 2,368 SiPM pixels read out by the CITIROC ASIC, enabling fast, low-power signal extraction. These features guided the design of a compact and robust Peltier-based focal-plane thermal-control system, which eliminates the need for external liquid cooling, while the SiPM bias system provides the high currents needed for high-duty-cycle observations under elevated Night Sky Background conditions. The Back-End Electronics manages all operations and achieves sub-nanosecond synchronization via the White Rabbit system. Initial results confirm that the ASTRI camera design meets the scientific and operational requirements for full array deployment.

Items.Authors: Camilo E. Jiménez Ángel, Ditte Slumstrup, Antonio L. Cabrera Lavers, Daniel Reverte Payá, José A. Rodríguez Losada, Víctor Rodríguez Herreros, Juan J. Fernández-Valdivia, Alfonso G. Cardell Bilbao
Items.Title: Fully Autonomous Data Processing for the GTC: The DRAGO System
Items.Abstract: The DRAGO system is a fully automated platform that executes the Data Reduction Process (DRP) for all GTC instruments without human intervention. It transforms raw data into standardized scientific products through automated orchestration, intelligent workflow management, and robust reprocessing. DRAGO is DRP-agnostic, integrating pipelines in any format or programming language. Its core functions include automatic observing block detection, calibration management, autonomous DRP configuration, and standardized output generation. These operate within a scalable architecture featuring data management, process scheduling, automatic quality control, and a user interface with API access. DRAGO enables fast, reliable, and reproducible reductions, representing a major step toward fully autonomous data handling in modern observatories.

Items.Authors: Satoki Matsushita, Keiichi Asada, Chih-Wei Huang, Cristina Romero-Canizales, Nimesh Patel, Jongho Park, Britton Jeter, Minchul Kam, Rema J. Ahmid, Pierre Martin-Cocher, Cheng-Yu Kuo, Jun Yi Koay, Ming-Tang Chen, Chih-Chiang Han, Derek Kubo, Yu-Chieh Huang, Philippe Raffin, Shu-Hao Chang, Ta-Shun Wei, Jia-Ruei Nian, Pai-An Chen, Peter Oshiro, Sally Lau, Timothy Norton, Tirupati K. Sridharan, Ramprasad Rao, Jacob Hawthorne, Keara Carter, Sheperd Doeleman, Jose Soto, Hannah Rana, Thomas R. Greve, Paul Ho
Items.Title: Science operation and status updates of the Greenland Telescope (GLT)
Items.Abstract: Primary scientific goal of the Greenland Telescope (GLT) project is to image black hole shadows using (sub)millimeter-wave Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) technique together with other (sub)millimeter telescopes around the world. It has a 12-m diameter dish, and operating at frequencies of 86, 230, and 345 GHz. It is currently located at the Pituffik Space Base (former Thule Air Base), and is regularly joining VLBI observations, such as Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and Global Millimeter VLBI Array (GMVA). In parallel, we accumulated data on pointing, aperture efficiency measurements, etc., at all three frequencies. We recently upgraded the receiver optics, and confirmed that all the receivers have almost the same focus positions and the pointings, which is the first step for the simultaneous multi-frequency operation. We also performed photogrammetry and holography to improve the surface accuracy. Here, we will report the latest activities and telescope characteristics.

Items.Authors: Solvay A. Blomquist, Hyukmo Kang, Maggie Kautz, Simran Agarwal, Kelsey Miller, Kyle Van Gorkom, Corey Fucetola, Heejoo Choi, Patrick Ingraham, Ewan S. Douglas, Daewook Kim, Sanchit Sabhlok, Alex Kupersmith, Adam Schilperoort
Items.Title: Tiny Observatory for Telescope Optimization (TOTO): testing algorithms for autonomous on-orbit alignment for space-based telescope systems
Items.Abstract: The Tiny Observatory for Telescope Optimization (TOTO) is an optical testbed designed to evaluate the efficacy of autonomously driven alignment algorithms for space-based telescope systems. For space-based missions, active control of the telescope on-orbit offers potential to relax passive alignment requirements and reduce on-ground verification activity. TOTO is used to evaluate and verify simulation work of two primary alignment algorithms, Stochastic Parallel Gradient Descent (SPGD) and focus-diverse phase retrieval. Previous simulation work has confirmed that by using SPGD for coarse alignment followed by focus-diverse phase retrieval for fine alignment, we can reach diffraction-limited performance on-orbit. This paper presents the results of the autonomous alignment algorithm of a TMA using TOTO. We report the current status of TOTO as well as preliminary results from SPGD and phase retrieval on the testbed using monochromatic light source to simulate a natural guide star.

Items.Authors: Lun-Jun Liu, Reinier Janssen, Jonathon Hunacek, Talia Saeid, Justin Bracks, Steve Hailey-Dunsheath, Shubh Agrawal, Charles Bradford, James Aguirre, Hrushi Athreya, Brockton Brendal, Bruce Bumble, Jeffrey Filippini, Jianyang Fu, Karolina Garcia, Christopher Groppi, Dylan Joralmon, Wooseok Kang, Garrett Keating, Ryan Keenan, Ian Lowe, Alex Manduca, Daniel Marrone, Philip Mauskopf, Evan Mayer, Sydnee O'Donnell, Simon Tartakovsky, Mathilde Van Cuyck, Joaquin Vieira, Jessica Zebrowski
Items.Title: Characterization of the laser-trimmed 317-420 μm KID array for the Terahertz Intensity Mapper
Items.Abstract: We present improved performance of the kinetic inductance detector (KID) array for the Terahertz Intensity Mapper (TIM). TIM is NASA-funded balloon mission aimed at probing the peak of cosmic star formation. The TIM payload is equipped with two spectral bands, 240–420 μm and 317–420 μm, each employing a focal plane of four-kilopixel wafers of lumped-element KIDs. Previous characterization of the 317–420 μm arrays revealed resonator collisions in the readout band, limiting the number of usable detectors and motivating optimization of resonator frequency spacing. To increase the number of science usable KIDs, here we present a strategy to redistribute resonator frequencies and apply laser trimming to shorten a small length of the resonator’s interdigitated capacitor. Measurements of the trimmed array show substantial improvement in frequency spacing and in the fraction of resonators meeting science requirements. In addition, we discuss planned refinements for subsequent TIM KID arrays.

Items.Authors: Branden Allen
Items.Title: Initial detector characterization and performance for the Portable Lunar Observer for Volatiles, Environment, and Resources (PLOVER)
Items.Abstract: The Portable Lunar Observer for Volatiles, Environment, and Resources (PLOVER) was conceived as a multi-use instrument package consisting of three instruments: (1) the Wide-band Internal Neutron and Gamma-ray Spectrometer (WINGS) a large-volume CLYC-based scintillator detector which is simultaneously sensitive to, and capable of detecting and discriminating between incident X/γ-rays and neutrons; (2) The Advanced Visible Infrared Analytic Spectrometer (AVIANS) a VIS/IR hyperspectral imager for simultaneous interrogation of surface mineralogy, and (3) CZT Advanced Imager for the Lunar Surface (TAILS) a high-resolution Compton imager to resolve nearby anomalies in the composition of the lunar surface.    Here we discuss the overall instrument design and deployment opportunities, expected performance and prospects, as well as the initial testing of the CLYC detectors in the laboratory and in the field at the summit of Maunakea.

Items.Authors: Tommaso Ghigna, Thomas Essinger-Hileman, Shoken Myozen, Tomotake Matsumura, Federico Trucchia, Mario Zannoni
Items.Title: 3D Printed W-band antennas for space applications
Items.Abstract: Additive manufacturing offers a promising route for compact, lightweight, and cost-effective antennas for next-generation space instruments. We present the design, fabrication, and characterization of a W-band (70–110 GHz) horn antenna produced using two additive approaches: a conductive-polymer process and titanium powder selective laser melting. We outline the workflow from design and print optimization to post-processing. Electromagnetic performance is evaluated through W-band radiation-pattern measurements with a VNA and compared with simulations. Beam profiles, gain, sidelobes, and cross-polarization are examined to reveal impacts of material properties and fabrication tolerances. The polymer horn demonstrates feasible low-mass, low-cost rapid prototyping, while the metal horn provides higher conductivity and thermal stability for cryogenic or space use. Challenges and prospects for space deployment are discussed.

Items.Authors: Jaime Ruíz-Díaz-Soto, Jorge Fuentes-Fernandez, Fernando Angeles, José Leonardo Garces, Alejandro Farah, Sebastian F. Sanchez
Items.Title: 3D printing in astronomy: mechanical design and optomechanical solutions using precision additive manufacturing in the EBANO instrument
Items.Abstract: The ÉBANO spectrograph stands out for its innovative design and fabrication using additive manufacturing (3D printing). Approximately 70% of its optomechanical components are manufactured from engineering polymers, meeting all scientific requirements. The mechanical design is based on flexible tolerances, which allowed the entire system to be manufactured using precision 3D printing. This approach significantly reduced cost, mass, and production time compared to traditional methods, while simplifying design adjustments and maintaining excellent optical performance. This work presents the design, FEA simulations, manufacturing process, assembly, and verification of these components, demonstrating the feasibility of additive manufacturing for high-quality astronomical instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Jie Liu
Items.Title: A 0.3–5 GHz low‑power cryogenic amplifier based on SiGe HBT technology for large‑scale detector arrays
Items.Abstract: We are developing low-power cryogenic low-noise amplifiers (LNAs) based on SiGe HBT technology. The amplifier is designed with a power consumption as low as 3 mW, making it suitable for direct integration into next-generation large pixel count receivers without inducing significant thermal load on superconducting detectors. Small-signal and noise model parameters of the HBT transistor were extracted at cryogenic temperatures (4 K). Based on this circuit model, we designed a 0.3–5 GHz cryogenic low-noise amplifier. Experimental results show that the amplifier achieves a typical gain of 37 dB and a noise temperature of approximately 6 K at ambient temperature of 4 K. The amplifier exhibits broadband characteristics with a bandwidth of about 5 GHz, which is advantageous for cryogenic readout systems, particularly for large pixel count KID detectors.

Items.Authors: Edoardo Borciani, Riccardo Campana, Fabio Muleri, Giuseppe Baldazzi, Claudio Labanti, Ezequiel J. Marchesini, Enrico Virgilli, Lorenzo Amati, Giulia Mattioli, Paolo Calabretto, Smiriti Srivastava, Ajay Sharma, Alfonso Pisapia, Farangis Takdehghan
Items.Title: A 3D Compton Polarimeter: the SWIPE mission concept
Items.Abstract: We present the development of a prototype for SWIPE (Soft-X and -ray WIde-field polarimeter) mission concept, which integrates photoelectric (0.2–8 keV) and Compton (20–200 keV) polarimeters for transient astrophysics. The novel Compton polarimeter utilizes scintillator bars coupled to double-ended readout electronics (Si-PM/SDDs). This configuration allows the reconstruction of the Depth of Interaction (DOI). Direct DOI knowledge enables reconstructing the polar scattering angle, and thus of the full scattering kinematics, optimizing the minimum detectable polarization. We report experimental tests of this approach, including DOI performance, spatial and energy resolution.

Items.Authors: Guillermo Martin, Louis Gemmerlé, Manon Lallement, Myriam Bonduelle, Jean-Philippe Berger, Roland Salut, Laurent Robert, Nadege Courjal, Germain Garreau, Denis Defrère
Items.Title: A 4T mid IR, double Bracewell, beam combiner in lithium niobate for high contrast interferometry
Items.Abstract: A novel 4 telescope beam combiner photonic chip, using a Lithium Niobate based technological platform in the mid IR, has been developed. These chips are devoted for instruments such as ASGAARD-NOTT for VLTI [1], METIS for EELT [2] or future spatial projects such as LIFE [3]. The single mode targeted spectral region is the L’-Band (3.4 - 4.1um). The goal of this work is to study the performances of the photonic chip: transmission, polarization behavior and achromaticity within this band. In particular, we will focus on the coupling ratio obtained in the directional couplers, the rejection ratio achieved and its spectral bandwidth. This different results were obtained using a 2T nulling bench developed at IPAG [4], and the 4T nulling bench developed at KU Leuven [5]

Items.Authors: Jason E. Williams, Nicholas P. Konidaris, Vincent Kowal, Alan Uomoto, Tyson S. Hare
Items.Title: A broadband, spectrophotometrically stable, light source for testing astronomical photometers
Items.Abstract: Instruments on the next generation telescopes will have unprecedented abilities to perform high precision spectrophotometry. In particular, detecting atmospheres around small-temperate exoplanets requires spectrophotometric precision on the order of parts-per-million. Therefore, designing a light source that allows for the assessment of the spectrophotometric performance of these instruments is crucial. To that end, we have developed a method to improve the spectrophotometric stability of an off-the-shelf current controlled light source. By controlling the temperature of the light source, we are able to improve the spectrophotometric precision by an order of magnitude, routinely down to less than 10 parts-per-million.

Items.Authors: N. P. S. Mithun, Hitesh Kumar L. Adalja, Arpit Patel, Deepak Kumar Painkra, A. Shivam, Bhavesh Raj Singh Nehra, Ajay Ratheesh, B. S. Bharath Saiguhan, C. S. Vaishnava, M. Shanmugam, Santoshv Vadawale
Items.Title: A collimated hard X-ray Compton polarimeter for solar flare observations from a small satellite platform
Items.Abstract: We present the design of a compact collimated hard X-ray Compton polarimeter operating in the energy range of ~20 - 200 keV, suitable for polarimetric studies of solar flares from a small satellite platform. The instrument consists of a plastic scintillator coupled with a photomultiplier tube (PMT) at the center and 12 high-Z scintillators read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPM) at two ends, placed around the plastic detector. Valid Compton scattering events from the plastic detector are identified by coincidence between interactions in that detector and one of the surrounding detectors. From the recorded azimuthal angle distribution of scattered photons, the degree of polarization and polarization angle can be measured. Here, we present the detailed design of the hard X-ray polarimeter, including simulations to estimate the instrument's sensitivity, the status of development and testing for each subsystem, and future plans.

Items.Authors: Ian P. McLean, Jeremy T. Lin, Pradip Gatkine
Items.Title: A compact high-performance imaging platform for NIR photonic instrumentation
Items.Abstract: This work presents a compact, thermally stabilized imaging platform designed for NIR photonic-chip integration and low-light astronomical or remote-sensing applications. The system uses staged thermoelectric coolers, heat pipes, and custom control electronics to maintain stable temperatures during long exposures. Stray light is reduced with broadband-absorbent materials, black-anodized surfaces, internal baffles, and low-reflection lens and filter holders. A light-sealed lens interface suppresses scattering from threaded elements, while vibration-damping structures improve mechanical stability. Custom acquisition software manages exposure settings, thermal states, and calibration steps, providing transparency into system behavior and enabling flexible spectral-analysis workflows. Initial tests show reduced thermal noise, suppressed internal reflections, and improved signal-to-noise ratios, demonstrating a strong foundation for future compact photonic instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Cristian Manzoni, Matteo Corti, Fabrizio Preda, Antonio Perri, Giulio Cerullo, Gianluca Valentini, Ondřej Ballada, Čestmír Barta
Items.Title: A compact hyperspectral camera for remote sensing from the ultraviolet to the thermal infrared
Items.Abstract: We introduce a compact hyperspectral camera based on the time-domain Fourier-transform approach, equipped with an ultrastable birefringent interferometer. The time-domain approach enables hyperspectral imaging with shorter acquisition times and higher spectral accuracy compared to standard dispersive optics. We provide experimental proofs of the camera capability by performing remote-sensing measurements in the visible and near-infrared range. Recently we extended the spectral range to the thermal infrared, where vibrational transitions associated with chemical bonds have their absorption. Due to its compactness, lightweight and extreme stability even in harsh environments, the camera is a unique enabling technology for remote unambiguous chemical identification.

Items.Authors: Keara J. Carter, C. Edward Tong, Gabriella Montano
Items.Title: A cryogenic dielectric stack optical diplexer for the wideband Submillimeter Array and beyond
Items.Abstract: We present a low-loss cryogenic optical diplexer, based on a multilayer dielectric stack, developed for the wideband Submillimeter Array (wSMA). Simultaneous dual-polarization multi-frequency capability is essential for next-generation submillimeter astronomy, improving calibration through Frequency Phase Transfer, expanding time-domain science, and increasing telescope efficiency. As part of the wSMA upgrade, which includes new dual-polarization receivers spanning 210-360 GHz, the diplexer is mounted in a 60 K filter wheel and operates at a 30° incidence angle. It serves as a low-pass filter enabling simultaneous multi-band observations within a shared optical path. We summarize its design and performance, including measurements using hot/cold load tests, a quasi-optical vector network analyzer, and a comb-injection method. Results show low loss and stable cryogenic behavior, supporting multi-frequency, dual-polarization observing for the wSMA and future instruments such as the ngEHT.

Items.Authors: Colin Cunningham, Carolyn Atkins, Gilles Bailet, Beth Biller, Mark McCaughrean, Colin McInnes, Stephen Todd
Items.Title: A giant telescope manufactured in space?
Items.Abstract: We explore a concept for a giant telescope manufactured in space to enable a primary mirror of 100m diameter. This is combined with a module containing a secondary mirror, correction optics and a prime focus instrumentation, flying in formation at about 1000m from the primary mirror. We assume that deployment of such a large primary mirror in space would require that a large fraction of the system would need to be manufactured in space in order to minimise launch costs, although that trade-off may now be changing with potential advances in heavy-lift capabilities. The enormous challenges of such a project mean that it would be many decades before the technology is possible, but when it is we could have unprecedented angular resolution and sensitivity and consequent breakthroughs in many areas, with exoplanet characterisation being the stand out application. Potential technical solutions are presented, leading to discussion of the potential scientific capability.

Items.Authors: Louis H. Marting, Kenichi Karatsu, Leon G. G. Olde Scholtenhuis, Shahab O. Dabironezare, Arend Moerman, David J. Thoen, Ton J. van der Linden, Akira Endo, Jochem J. A. Baselmans
Items.Title: A high efficiency filterbank using directional filters for integral field spectrometers in the millimeter/sub-millimeter band
Items.Abstract: Superconducting on-chip spectrometers are advancing rapidly, and large imaging spectrometers are quickly becoming feasible in the sub-mm band. These imaging spectrometers are ideally equipped to advance our understanding of several exciting astronomical signals that describe the evolution of our Universe. This includes SZ effect observations, CMB polarimetry, LIM and tomography of terahertz line-emitting galaxies (TLEG). These science cases all require imaging spectrometers with moderate spectral resolution and a large bandwidth, however, the state-of-the-art sub-mm instruments have come short in reaching the required sensitivity.    In this contribution, we experimentally demonstrate a new type of filter for on-chip spectrometers, called a directional filter, with a measured filter efficiency of 75%. This filter improves upon the conventionally used half-wave filters, which typically have an efficiency of 25% or less. We aim to implement this design on the TIFUUN instrument.

Items.Authors: Homin Jiang, Bishnu K. Sharma
Items.Title: A high‑speed direct RF sampling FPGA platform for high-frequency radio telescope backends
Items.Abstract: High-speed ADCs operating at GSps rates enable the direct digitization of wideband RF signals, significantly reducing reliance on complex analog downconversion chains. This approach minimizes distortion and phase noise while extending spectral coverage. Recent advances, such as Altera’s integration of 8-bit ADCs capable of sampling at up to 64 GSps, support bandwidths exceeding 32 GHz and greatly simplify the IF section.  We present the development of a 64 GSps high-speed digitization system based on Altera’s Direct RF FPGA platform, utilizing the Stratix 10 AX FPGA evaluation kit. The platform incorporates 64 GSps ADC chiplets and an embedded Direct RF IP core. Preliminary testing with a 26.5 GHz wideband noise source and notch filter demonstrates promising performance in 64 GSps mode. This system represents a significant step toward next-generation digital backends and will be well-suited for high-frequency radio telescopes such as the JCMT and the GLT.

Items.Authors: Thomas M. Herbst, José R. Sánchez-Gallego
Items.Title: A low cost, thermal infrared, all-sky cloud camera
Items.Abstract: We describe the design, construction, and testing of a compact, thermal infrared, all-sky camera based on commercial radiometric modules from FLIR. Five wide-angle Lepton 3.1r cameras provide full sky coverage above 30° elevation with ~0.5° spatial resolution. A 6th camera would allow full, hemispheric imaging. The entire system requires only a single Power Over Ethernet connection and fits within a 20 cm weatherproof housing. Using 3D-printed components and a simple NUC-type linux computer, the total cost of the all-sky camera is approximately €1000.

Items.Authors: Christopher S. Benson, Patrick Ashworth, Peter S. Barry, Harry Gordon-Moys, Izaak Morris
Items.Title: A low-noise Fourier transform survey spectrometer leveraging on-chip spectrometers
Items.Abstract: The development of wide-FoV medium-resolution (R=1000-3000) mapping spectrometers has been identified as a priority in millimetre/sub-millimeter astronomy for future and existing facilities. Mapping spectrometer architectures that have been historically used for medium-R mapping spectroscopy have significant technical hurdles to overcome. To combat the inherent noise in Fourier Transform Spectrometers (FTSs) due to their spectral multiplexing and achieve an effective R~2000 mapping spectrometer in the near-term, we propose combining a medium-R FTS with a low-resolution on-chip filterbank spectrometer focal plane as a post-dispersion mechanism. In this arrangement, an FBS with R~100-200 is sufficient to dramatically improve mapping speeds without compromising the fundamental imaging advantages of the FTS. We present our progress in the laboratory validation of this spectrometer architecture and discuss projected performance from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope as an example.

Items.Authors: Takumi Izawa, Kosuke Aizawa, Ryosuke Akizawa, Scott Cray, Samuel Dietterich, Shaul Hanany, Jürgen Koch, Rex Lam, Asuka Maeda, Tomotake Matsumura, Ryota Takaku
Items.Title: A millimeter-wave transmission measurement system for optical samples cooled to liquid-nitrogen temperature
Items.Abstract: Characterizing optical materials at cryogenic temperatures is crucial for millimeter-wave astronomical receivers. We developed a transmittance measurement system using a liquid-nitrogen cryostat and a vector-network analyzer (VNA). A sample inside the cryostat is cooled to 94 K via a copper strap, while millimeter waves from the VNA pass through a Zotefoam window. A rotatable sample holder allows measurements with and without the sample in a single cryostat run. We measured the transmittance of a 50-mm-diameter, 99.5% purity alumina disk between 140 and 220 GHz at room temperature and 94 K. The refractive index and loss tangent changed from n = 3.083±0.002 and tanδ = (3.6±0.1)×10-4 at room temperature, to n = 3.059±0.002 and tanδ = (0.0±0.1)×10-4 at 94 K.

Items.Authors: Jensen Hoy, Giorgio Savini, Shana Sullivan, Tsz Chiu, Vrinda Singhal, Thomas Schlichter
Items.Title: A modified cots near-UV folded Czerny-Turner spectrometer for CubeSat OB-star monitoring
Items.Abstract: This work describes a compact near-UV Czerny–Turner spectrometer and flatsat demonstrator built entirely from commercial optics and opto-mechanics for future use on a 4U CubeSat. Starting from an existing astigmatism-free bicylinder design (Q. Zhou and Z. Zou, 2022), we re-optimise the spectrometer for the 300-330 nm OB-star band and convert the prescription into a manufacturable assembly using adjustable clamps and 3D-printed prototypes. A Raspberry-Pi-based flatsat stack then acquires spectra and runs a C pipeline that fits line centroids, widths, and fluxes for low-bit-rate downlink. We will present measured resolving power and throughput and discuss lessons for re-using optimised COTS spectrographs in UV small-satellite missions.

Items.Authors: Denis Tcherniak, Klavs Rommedahl, Gabriel Cobos Tello, Irfan Kuvvetli, Carol Anne Oxborrow, Desiree Della Monica Ferreira
Items.Title: A modular and mission agnostic EGSE concept for testing of astronomical space instruments: as applied to NewAthena and Theseus missions
Items.Abstract: We present a standardized, modular Electrical Ground Support Equipment (EGSE) architecture for functional testing of space mission electronics. This system features a reusable controller module and mission-specific modules, all within a 19” rack form factor and powered via Power over Ethernet. Standardized interfaces and REST API control enable rapid adaptation to different devices under test. This approach significantly reduces development time and cost, allowing small engineering teams to efficiently support diverse missions by focusing only on mission-specific requirements.

Items.Authors: Benjamin Boyd, Bryce Warren, Steve Benton, Ajay S. Gill, John Hartley, Bradley Holder, William Jones, Steven Li, C. Barth Netterfield, Emaad Paracha, Susan Redmond, Javier Romualdez, Simon Tartakovsky, Philippe Voyer, Adyn Miles
Items.Title: A modular dynamics simulation framework for the pre-assembly validation of airborne telescope control systems
Items.Abstract: Modern high-altitude astronomical payloads integrate increasingly lightweight structures and complex control systems, making early-stage performance prediction essential for informed design decisions. We present a fully modular, real-time simulation framework developed to evaluate payload behavior before hardware integration, and to provide a consistent system-level environment for mechanical design, hardware selection, and control-strategy development. The simulator is organized around a configurable architecture in which every payload is described by a specification of bodies, joints, actuators, and sensors, enabling alterations to system topology with little overhead. We demonstrate this framework through the validation of the Gigapixel Balloon-borne Imaging Telescope (GigaBIT) flight software in a representative closed-loop dynamics simulation. This approach supports early validation of design concepts, reduces integration risk, and offers a path toward more robust instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Luca Baldini, Ronaldo Bellazzini, Augusto Cattafesta, Juan Sebastian Hincapie Tarquino, Luca Latronico, Alberto Manfreda, Massimo Minuti, Melissa Pesce-Rollins, Alessandro Profeti, Carmelo Sgrò, Stefano Silvestri
Items.Title: A monolithic gas pixel detector with printed-on-chip multiplication stage for astronomical X-ray polarimetry
Items.Abstract: We present a new gas pixel detector (GPD) concept for astronomical X-ray polarimetry in which the charge-multiplication stage is integrated onto the readout chip by adding two thin, patterned layers above its top metal plane. These, together with the ASIC surface, form a micro-gap-like electron-multiplier structure, now fully monolithic, with a single silicon die acting at the same time as a gas multiplier, charge-collecting anode, and readout electronics. Due to the the sub-micron accuracy of the underlying process and the minimal exposed dielectric, this new class of polarization-sensitive detectors has the potential to improve over the previous generation of GPDs in all key areas, including spurious modulation and time stability.    We have realized and operated several gain structures, both on test substrates and on actual pixelated ASICs, down to 43 micron pitch, and we shall present a full characterization of such devices in terms of gain, energy resolution and time stability.
